title: We’ve Filed More Than 50 Legal Claims Over Abuse by Federal Immigration Agents. Here's Why.
summary: Federal immigration agents are committing civil liberties abuses across the country — our FTCA filings are taking them to task.
body_text: Back to News & Commentary We’ve Filed More Than 50 Legal Claims Over Abuse by Federal Immigration Agents. Here's Why. The claimants detail being unlawfully detained, denied medical care, or targeted simply for speaking out or recording what they saw. Their experiences reveal a dangerous pattern of abuse that threatens the rights and safety of us all. Yasmin Cader , she/her , ACLU Share This Page August 5, 2026 In April, ICE held one mother, who was five months pregnant, with her husband and four children, including her 11-month-old baby, in a cell with no sunlight and little access to running water for nearly a month. The mother lost consciousness twice from the heat before anyone took her seriously. “My children were confused and scared about why they were trapped in this cell, why they could not go outside, and why they had no toys to play with,” said the mother, who is unnamed here due to her immigration status. On July 29, ACLU affiliates announced the filing of 54 federal tort claims against the federal government on behalf of people and families harmed by federal immigration agents across 17 states and Washington, D.C. Like the story of the pregnant mother, each claim reveals the story of someone whose rights were violated by federal law enforcement since President Donald Trump took office again. Some were seriously injured, while others were unlawfully detained, denied medical care, or targeted simply for speaking out or recording what they saw. Together, their experiences reveal a dangerous and widespread pattern of abuse that threatens the rights and safety of us all. Campaign Aug 2026 Immigrants' Rights +2 Issues The People v. Agents of Chaos and Cruelty Federal law enforcement have abused and terrorized countless people. We must demand justice for their victims. Explore campaign The People V. Agents Of Chaos And Cruelty. Explore Campaign. Campaign Aug 2026 Immigrants' Rights +2 Issues The People v. Agents of Chaos and Cruelty Federal law enforcement have abused and terrorized countless people. We must demand justice for their victims. The People V. Agents Of Chaos And Cruelty. Explore Campaign. Since President Trump took office again, immigration agents have terrorized communities in workplaces, schools and neighborhoods across the country. Masked agents have smashed car windows and dragged people from their vehicles, separated parents from their children, ignored documents proving lawful immigration status, and detained people in dangerous facilities without urgently needed medical care. U.S. citizens and noncitizens alike have been detained, and in some cases, assaulted based on nothing more than how they look or sound. The Trump administration has also targeted U.S. citizens for simply exercising their First Amendment rights and speaking out against federal agents’ abuses. The consequences of this violence and abuse have been devastating. Many people have suffered serious injuries and property damage, and some have lost their lives. In January, ICE shot and killed Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis. Months later, federal agents shot and killed two men in July: Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas and Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine. More than 50 people have also died in ICE detention since the start of President Trump’s mass deportation campaign. What's a Federal Tort Claim? Such abuses are widespread and systemic, reflecting a coordinated effort to intimidate and control our communities. They require a coordinated response. That’s why the ACLU and our affiliates are taking legal action under the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA). The Federal Tort Claims Act allows a person to seek financial compensation from the federal government if a federal employee hurts them while on the job. Filing a claim is the first step people need to take before they can have their day in court. Without the FTCA, the government would be almost entirely shielded from lawsuits for monetary damages. It is one of the few paths available for someone harmed by a federal agent to hold the government financially accountable, even when the individual officer is never identified or disciplined. We’re using the FTCA to seek accountability and compensation for the abuse our clients experienced at the government’s hands. The People Behind Our Campaign Against Federal Immigration Abuses The 54 stories at the center of this campaign paint a horrifying picture of the terror that federal agents have inflicted on our communities. In one case, armed, masked agents surrounded Willy Wender Aceituno, a U.S. citizen from North Carolina, outside a restaurant and forced to prove his citizenship. After Aceituno showed the officers identification confirming his citizenship, the officers walked away — only to return minutes later to smash his car window and throw him onto broken glass. They handcuffed Aceituno, placed him in an unmarked SUV, and eventually left him bleeding on the side of the road, miles from his car. Press Release Jul 2026 Immigrants' Rights An Assault on Due Process: Frontline Legal Service Providers Sound the Alarm as the Collapse of Legal Representation for Thousands of Unaccompanied Children Nears WASHINGTON – Today, in a press briefing hosted by the Defending Our Neighbors Fund, frontline legal service providers across the country warned that legal representation for thousands of unaccompanied immigrant children is at risk of total collapse as the federal contract that funds immigrant children’s access to lawyers expires on July 31, 2026. Since November 2025, the Trump Administration has withheld payment from legal service providers representing unaccompanied children in an effort to force them to turn over sensitive, privileged information about the children they represent. In response, the Defending Our Neighbors Fund has provided emergency funding to support several frontline legal service providers’ ability to continue representing their clients; however, without immediate federal action to renew the federal contract, tens of thousands of unaccompanied immigrant children are at imminent risk of losing access to legal representation and will be forced to self-represent against trained government attorneys. Michael Lukens, Executive Director of the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, said: “The government knows exactly what it is doing. A child’s best chance at due process is to have an attorney by their side—it’s why this program exists. By refusing to pay for services already provided, the government is deliberately undermining the very protections these children are entitled to.” Melissa Lopez, Executive Director of Estrella del Paso, said: “Over the course of 20 years, this network of legal service providers has developed a unique level of expertise working with children who have experienced trauma. We have spent 20 years building this institutional knowledge that we are going to lose on Friday. There is no replacing the organizations providing these services. We know what happens to children that go to court without an attorney. In one word, it is deportation. The government is trying to eliminate our work and this program because they know that without attorneys, children will be deported.” Meena Shah, Managing Director of Legal Services at The Door, said: “Children could not need legal representation more than they do right now. Judges are moving forward, with or without representation. They will order children deported without representation, starting Monday morning, across the United States. None of us want to abandon our clients, and we will do our utmost to fight for their lawful pursuit of a fair proceeding.” Lindsay Toczylowski, CEO and Co-Founder of the Immigrant Defenders Law Center, said: “When you take lawyers away from children, you do not just take away legal representation—you remove one of the few meaningful checks on government misconduct. The attacks on immigrant children and their advocates are not an isolated policy failure or a simple contract dispute. It is part of a broader effort to dismantle the legal protections, oversight mechanisms, and constitutional safeguards that stand in the way of unchecked government power.” Mayra Peters-Quintero, Executive Director at Abundant Futures Fund and Co-Lead at Defending Our Neighbors Fund, said: “Justice shouldn’t have a price tag. It should be available to anyone, regardless of age or income. We launched the Defending Our Neighbors Fund because we understood that the American public, regardless of political orientation, agrees on this basic principle. Yet countless children–even as young as babies–must face trained prosecutors without a lawyer by their side and the crisis is about to get much worse. Through the Fund, everyday Americans are stepping up to help fund legal access, turning their outrage into action, and despair into defense.” ### Created in partnership with United We Dream Network (UWD) and the ACLU, The Defending Our Neighbors Fund is hosted at Abundant Futures Fund, a fiscally sponsored project of Rockefeller Philanthropy Advisors. The Fund is focused on fundraising, identifying grantees, and rapidly distributing resources to organizations working on the frontlines to support immigrant communities through legal representation and, when possible, bond assistance. Press Release Jul 2026 Immigrants' Rights Criminal Law Reform ACLU Affiliates File More Than 50 Legal Claims Against the Federal Government on Behalf of People Harmed by Federal Law Enforcement NEW YORK — The American Civil Liberties Union announced today that its affiliates have now filed 54 claims in 17 states and Washington, D.C. against the federal government on behalf of people who have suffered serious violence, abuse, and neglect at the hands of federal law enforcement. Since the beginning of President Trump’s second term, federal law enforcement agents have terrorized communities and people in their custody with a blatant disregard for the law. The consequences have been deadly. Conditions in ICE facilities are so inhumane that the rate of deaths in ICE custody has more than doubled since Trump’s term began, reaching its highest level in over a decade. In early July, reporting revealed that, after the White House pushed to increase arrest rates, ICE officials detained more than 10,000 people in five days. Only days later, ICE agents in unmarked vehicles shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas while he was on his way to work. The following week, a federal agent shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine. Across the country, ACLU affiliates are fighting back against the Trump administration’s illegal conduct by filing claims under the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA), one of the few legal tools available to seek financial compensation for wrongdoing by federal government employees. Through this coordinated effort, ACLU affiliates are representing dozens of people and families who are seeking justice for the harm they experienced at the hands of federal immigration agents. “As more than 50 of these cases show, federal agents’ violence, misconduct and utter disregard for the law is rampant,” said Yasmin Cader, deputy executive director of the ACLU. “President Trump and his law enforcement officers rely on a perceived sense of impunity, but no one is above the law. This administration is making everyone in America less safe and less free. That’s why the ACLU and its affiliates are fighting back at every turn.” Each of the 54 claims that have been filed tells an individual story of someone who was brutalized by federal immigration agents. Together, they reveal a widespread pattern of civil rights violations and abuse carried out by officials nationwide, affecting people who are immigrants, U.S. citizens, lawful permanent residents, families, workers, and people exercising their constitutional rights. These claims put names and faces to the harm that federal law enforcement agencies have been inflicting in communities across the country. The people represented include: A mother, who was five months into a high-risk pregnancy when she was held with her four children, including her 11-month-old child, in a CBP facility for approximately four weeks. The family was held in a cell with limited access to clean running water and without any windows to the outside. Rodney, from Georgia, who was arrested by ICE agents with guns drawn while his two young children watched, and was later denied needed medical care and accessibility accommodations while in ICE custody. Willy, a U.S. citizen in North Carolina, who was on his way back from a restaurant when federal immigration agents racially profiled him, put him in a headlock, and threw him to the ground. Norma Bowe, a grandmother, professor of public health at Kean University, and registered nurse, who was assaulted in front of Delaney Hall by ICE agents while there to operate her mobile health clinic. Darren, a U.S. citizen from Illinois, who was arrested at work after DHS agents broke through a gate to reach him, after which he required hospitalization for the two chemical irritants they used against him and was left without any of his confiscated property. “My story is not just about what happened to me. It’s about the kind of country we choose to be,” said Darren, a U.S. citizen being represented by the ACLU of Illinois. “No one should lose their dignity the moment they come face to face with those who hold power.” Earlier this month, the ACLU released a report analyzing immigration enforcement actions in the first year of President Trump’s second term. The report, Agents of Chaos and Cruelty, examines more than 1,200 immigration enforcement incidents across eight states and found that more than 400 of those incidents involved misconduct by immigration agents, including excessive force, racial profiling, and intimidation and abuse. “I was violently attacked by ICE agents while I was trying to provide medical care for people visiting their loved ones in Delaney Hall,” said Dr. Norma Bowe, a registered nurse and professor of public health at Kean University being represented by the ACLU of New Jersey. “ICE agents are acting like they have impunity and are inflicting harm however and whenever they want; without accountability, more people will get hurt and die. ICE must be held responsible.” The ACLU and its affiliates will continue to work to defend the rights of everyone, including people harmed by Trump’s immigration forces, and hold the administration accountable for its unlawful and inhumane actions. title: Wavedash Summer Jam '26 Winners
summary: The Wavedash Summer Jam ran from July 17 to July 26, 2026. The theme, revealed the moment the jam opened, was BAD CONNECTION.
body_text: The Wavedash Summer Jam ran from July 17 to July 26, 2026. The theme, revealed the moment the jam opened, was BAD CONNECTION . Judging is now finished. Entries were scored on five criteria: alignment with theme, creativity, interactivity and gameplay, technical completeness, and use of the Wavedash platform, with bonus points for SDK features like leaderboards, achievements, and cloud saves. "Bad connection" turned out to be a wide open prompt. Across the top five alone it produced a séance switchboard, a data-center outbreak, a dating-app haunting, a physics run through public WiFi, and a blind date between two broken robots. Here are the top five, counting down from fifth place. 5. Dating.data by lenthesmiledev A dating sim about a blind date between two faulty robots. Rather than picking from a list of dialogue options, you drag words together to link them into what you're trying to say (communication as an assembly problem) which is a neat fit for a theme about signals not getting through. Play Dating.data → 4. Knock Knock by Stitched A horror game about finding love on a dating app while you move out of your apartment. Things start to go wrong when a bad connection from a previous date refuses to leave you alone. The only entry in the jam to read the theme as a horror premise. Play Knock Knock → 3. Packet Loss by sumukhjoshi75 A top-down survival game set in a data center during a server crisis. A virus spreads across 20 server racks in real time while your Data Pool drains. You patch infected racks, deploy antivirus towers, and use sprint bursts to reach whatever is failing next. Every 10 patches, the virus escalates, duplicating infections and jumping between adjacent racks. No scripted waves and no boss fights, just a difficulty curve you create yourself. Ships with 23 achievement categories and a competitive leaderboard. Play Packet Loss → 2. TTL8! by aria A terrible fate has befallen you… having to eat with no YouTube! A bouncy physics arcade game about braving the depths of "public WiFi" to restore your lost connection. Easy to bounce around in, considerably harder to route through a stage efficiently (which is where the leaderboard comes in). Play TTL8! → 1. Hold, Please — Grand Prize by Project Ditto You work nights at an afterlife telephone exchange. The living ring in wanting to speak to someone who died. They never say the name. They say 'my late mother, the one I miss most at Christmas,' and then they wait. You work out who the caller means from ten case files, then physically carry the telephone plugs across the floor to connect them. The lines can't cross. Too many live connections trips the breaker. Eight nights, three strikes each. It's a deduction puzzle built out of a switchboard, and it took the grand prize. Play Hold, Please → Prizes Place Game Prize 1st Hold, Please $1,000 2nd TTL8! $500 3rd Packet Loss $250 4th Knock Knock $125 5th Dating.data $75 Everyone who submitted a build receives $10 in Wavedash credits , usable on any game on the site, along with written feedback scored on the same rubric the judges used. Thank you to everyone who built something in ten days, and to everyone who played and voted along the way. All five winners run instantly in your browser. Another jam is coming. Join the Wavedash Discord to hear about it first.

title: How to Study for the Digital SAT: 6-Step Guide (2026)
summary: How to Study for the Digital SAT using a proven 6-step system: Bluebook diagnostic, error log, targeted drills, and Desmos tips. Start your plan now.
body_text: How to Study for the Digital SAT: 6-Step Guide (2026) TLDR The best way to study for the Digital SAT is not to grind through endless practice tests. Start with one full-length Bluebook diagnostic, review every missed question using a structured error log, drill your weakest skills by domain, and master the Bluebook interface (especially Desmos, Mark for Review, and the Option Eliminator). Practice tests measure your readiness. Score gains come from the targeted work you do between them. Most students studying for the Digital SAT hit the same wall early: they know Bluebook exists, they have heard of Khan Academy, they have maybe seen the Question Bank mentioned on Reddit, and they have no idea what order to use any of it. The vocabulary alone is confusing. Adaptive modules, active questions, content domains, score ranges. Every resource uses these terms like you should already know them. This guide fixes that. It defines the Digital SAT terms you keep seeing, explains what each one means for your study plan, and gives you a practical system for turning practice into actual score improvement. Before anything else, understand the core principle: a practice test tells you what broke. It does not fix it. The fix happens in the work between practice tests, when you classify mistakes, drill weak skills, and learn the digital tools that are now part of the exam itself. Take a free Digital SAT practice exam to establish your baseline before reading further. Quick Answer: How Should You Study for the Digital SAT? The most effective Digital SAT study plan is to take one official Bluebook practice test, identify your weakest content domains, review every mistake using an error log, practice those skills with Khan Academy and the College Board Student Question Bank, then retest every 2–3 weeks. Most students improve faster by reviewing mistakes than by taking more practice tests. Learning the Bluebook interface—including Desmos, Mark for Review, and the Option Eliminator—is also an essential part of preparation because these tools are available during the real exam. Who This Guide Is For This guide is designed for: First-time SAT students who don't know where to begin Students switching from the paper SAT Students retaking the SAT after a disappointing score Students targeting competitive college admissions Students studying independently without a tutor If you already have a structured SAT study plan, you can jump directly to the glossary or study schedules. What Makes the Digital SAT Different? The Digital SAT is shorter than the old paper SAT, but “shorter” does not mean “easier to prepare for.” The format demands a different set of habits. Here is what changed: The test runs through College Board’s Bluebook app, not a paper booklet. There are two sections: Reading and Writing, then Math. Each section is split into two modules. Performance on Module 1 determines whether you get a harder or easier Module 2. Built-in tools include a Desmos graphing calculator, Mark for Review, Option Eliminator, highlights, notes, a line reader, and a timer. These are available inside Bluebook for every test taker. Reading and Writing passages are shorter. Each question typically has its own short passage. The total test time is 2 hours and 14 minutes: 64 minutes for Reading and Writing and 70 minutes for Math . The format shift means that studying for the Digital SAT requires three layers of preparation, not just one. You need content knowledge (grammar rules, algebra, reading comprehension), format understanding (adaptive modules, timing, question types), and interface fluency (knowing how to actually use the Bluebook tools under pressure). Practitioners on LinkedIn have made this point directly: tutors who focus only on content while ignoring Bluebook tools like Desmos, annotation, and flagging are leaving points on the table. The interface is part of the test now. Digital SAT Format at a Glance Section Modules Questions Time Time per Question Reading and Writing 2 (32 min each) 54 64 minutes ~1 min 11 sec Math 2 (35 min each) 44 70 minutes ~1 min 35 sec Total 4 98 2 hr 14 min — The total score ranges from 400 to 1600, with each section scored from 200 to 800 . There is a 10-minute break between the two sections. The Digital SAT Study Loop Before jumping into glossary terms, here is the study system that should organize everything you do. Think of it as a loop you repeat, not a checklist you finish once. Diagnose. Take one full-length Bluebook practice test under real timing. Decode. Break your misses into domain, skill, and error type. Drill. Practice targeted skills with Khan Academy, the Question Bank, or targeted SAT problem sets . Explain. Write why each wrong answer was tempting and why the right answer works. Retest. Take another timed section or full test after enough study. Adjust. Move your study time toward the skills with the highest score payoff. College Board research found that completing Bluebook full-length practice tests is associated with higher SAT scores: about 25.7 points higher for one test, 45.5 for two, and 61.4 for three or more, compared with similar students who completed none. The study cautions these estimates are not causal , but the pattern is clear. Practice matters, and more structured practice matters more. How Much Can Your SAT Score Improve? Actual score improvement depends on your starting score, consistency, and the quality of your review. Starting Score Typical Improvement After Structured Study 900–1100 150–300 points 1100–1300 80–180 points 1300–1450 40–120 points 1450+ 20–70 points Students who consistently review mistakes, study weak domains, and take periodic official practice tests generally improve more than students who simply take repeated practice exams. Glossary of Digital SAT Study Terms This is the core of the guide. Each entry defines a term, explains why it matters, and tells you how to study with it. Digital SAT The current SAT format, administered digitally through College Board’s Bluebook app. It replaced the paper SAT and uses shorter sections, adaptive modules, and built-in tools. Do not rely on old paper SAT habits. Practice inside Bluebook and learn the interface before test day. Bluebook College Board’s digital testing app for the SAT, PSAT-related assessments, and some AP Exams. Bluebook is where you take official full-length practice tests and where you will take the real SAT. Use the Test Preview feature before your first full test. Take full-length practice tests under realistic timing. Review results in My Practice. Test Preview An untimed Bluebook feature with a short set of questions that lets you experience the digital format and tools without score pressure. It does not provide scores or feedback. Use it once before your diagnostic to lower interface anxiety. Do not count it as content study. Full-Length Practice Test A timed practice SAT inside Bluebook that simulates the full Digital SAT experience and produces a score. About 64% of SAT takers used full-length practice tests, and 93% of those users found them helpful, according to the same College Board research brief . Take one as a diagnostic, then retest only after targeted review. Do not stack practice tests back to back without studying in between. Diagnostic Test Your first realistic practice test, used to find your baseline score and weak skills. Without a diagnostic, students often waste time studying topics they already know. Take one Bluebook full-length practice test under real timing and conditions, then build an error log from the results. Baseline Score The score you earn before serious prep, usually from your diagnostic. It tells you how far you are from your target score and how aggressive your timeline needs to be. A student going from 1050 to 1250 needs a fundamentally different plan than one going from 1400 to 1500. Target Score The SAT score you are aiming for, based on your college list, scholarship goals, or personal benchmark. A “good SAT score” depends on where you are applying. Set a target total score and section scores. If your target is 1450 and your diagnostic is 1320, break the 130-point gap into Math and Reading/Writing priorities. Check your predicted SAT score to see where you stand and which sections need the most work. Adaptive Testing A test design where the difficulty of later modules changes based on earlier performance. On the Digital SAT, performance on Module 1 determines whether Module 2 is more difficult or less difficult . Take Module 1 seriously. Accuracy early in each section matters because it affects routing. Module 1 The first half of each section. Module 1 contains a broad mix of easy, medium, and hard questions. Your performance here determines which version of Module 2 you receive. Prioritize clean accuracy. Avoid careless mistakes. Use the final minutes to check flagged questions. Module 2 The second half of each section, routed based on Module 1 performance. A harder Module 2 can feel intimidating, but it likely means you did well on Module 1. Do not waste mental energy during the test trying to figure out which route you got. Practice harder timed sets during prep so a difficult Module 2 does not create panic. Content Domain A broad category of skills tested on the SAT. College Board breaks each section into domains with approximate weightings, which helps you prioritize study time. Tag each missed question by domain. If most of your misses are in Standard English Conventions or Advanced Math, that becomes your study priority. Skill A narrower tested ability within a domain, such as Boundaries, Words in Context, Systems of Equations, or Nonlinear Functions. Skills are more actionable than broad sections. “Improve Math” is vague. “Practice nonlinear functions and systems” is specific. Use Khan Academy or the Question Bank to drill one skill at a time. Student Question Bank College Board’s official practice question tool, which lets you filter SAT questions by section, domain, skill, and difficulty. It is one of the best sources for targeted official practice after a diagnostic. Use it after reviewing a Bluebook test. Filter to your weak skills instead of randomly grinding questions. Active Questions Questions in the Student Question Bank that are also included in currently active official full-length practice tests. If you see these questions before taking a Bluebook practice test, your practice score can become inflated because you have already seen the answers. This is a real concern. Practitioners on Reddit repeatedly discuss the overlap problem and recommend using the “Exclude Active Questions” filter when available. One thread specifically asked whether doing Question Bank questions before Bluebook tests makes scores inaccurate, and replies confirmed that repeated exposure can skew results. If you want clean practice-test scores, take at least one diagnostic before heavy Question Bank drilling. Khan Academy Official Digital SAT Prep Free official SAT prep created in partnership with College Board. It includes practice questions, videos, lessons, hints, and strategies . Use Bluebook for diagnostics and full-test simulation. Use Khan Academy to learn and drill skills between tests. Khan Academy explicitly notes that Bluebook is useful for practice tests and format familiarity but is not designed to teach all tested content by itself. Desmos The built-in graphing calculator available through Bluebook on the SAT. Desmos changes Digital SAT Math strategy because it can graph functions, find intersections, check roots, and support tables and regressions. One Reddit user reported jumping from a March 1450 to a June 1540, attributing the Math improvement largely to using Desmos for systems and similar problems, which left more time for harder questions and checking work. But Desmos is a tool, not magic. A tutor on LinkedIn made a useful point: students should not jump into Desmos strategy before learning the content. Once you know the math, then decide whether a problem is faster by hand or with the calculator. Mark for Review A Bluebook tool that lets you flag questions to revisit within the same module. It helps with pacing and prevents one hard question from wrecking an entire module. Use a rule: if a question is not moving after 60 to 90 seconds, make your best guess, mark it, and return if time remains. Option Eliminator A Bluebook tool that lets you cross out answer choices you think are wrong. It makes guessing more strategic and reduces the chance of re-reading choices you already rejected. Practice eliminating obviously wrong choices on Reading and Writing questions before choosing between the final two. Error Log A record of missed, guessed, and slow questions, including why the mistake happened. The error log turns practice into learning. More on how to build one in the review section below. Score Range A range shown on College Board score reports that indicates how much a score might vary across different administrations under identical conditions. It prevents overreacting to one practice score. Watch trends over several tests and sections, not one number. A Reddit thread of 1500+ scorers showed wide variation between practice and real scores. One user got 1390 on Practice Test 6 shortly before test day and 1520 on the actual June SAT. Another listed practice scores of 1590/1580/1590, then scored 1450 in March and 1540 in June. Treat a practice score as a readiness estimate, not a promise. Student-Produced Response A Math question where you type in your own answer instead of choosing from multiple-choice options. These questions remove the option of backsolving from answer choices, so you need clean setup and checking. Practice entering exact values, decimals, and fractions carefully. Use Desmos to verify when useful. Exam Setup The Bluebook process you complete before test day to prepare your registered SAT on your testing device. College Board says registered SAT Weekend students should complete exam setup 1 to 5 days before test day . Do not leave this for the morning of the test. Device Lending College Board’s process for students who need to borrow a testing device for SAT Weekend. You must request a device at least 30 days before test day, and approval is not guaranteed. Device planning belongs in your study calendar, not the final week. How to Take Your First Diagnostic The diagnostic is the most important single step in learning how to study for the Digital SAT. Everything else depends on it. Here is the process: Download Bluebook. Complete the Test Preview to learn the interface. Take one full-length Bluebook practice test under real conditions: timed, no pausing, quiet room, on the device you plan to test on if possible. After the test, review your results in My Practice. Record these details from your diagnostic: Total score and section scores Domain-level performance (which domains had the most misses) Every question you missed Every question you guessed on Every question where you were slow or unsure Any interface mistakes (forgot to use Desmos, ran out of time, did not use Mark for Review) This data drives everything that follows. How to Review a Digital SAT Practice Test Most guides say “review your mistakes.” That is too vague to be useful. Here is a system that actually works. Every wrong or slow question goes into one of four buckets: Content gap. You did not know the grammar rule, math concept, word meaning, or reading skill. Fix: learn the concept, then drill similar questions. Process error. You knew the concept but used the wrong method, skipped steps, failed to check units, or chose the slow path. Fix: practice the right approach on similar problems until it becomes automatic. Reading/wording trap. You missed a word like “not,” “least,” “best supported,” “per,” or “which choice completes the text.” Fix: slow down on prompts and train yourself to underline key words. Pacing/interface error. You ran out of time, failed to flag and return, lost track of modules, used Desmos inefficiently, or did not use the eliminator tools. Fix: timed Bluebook rehearsal with deliberate tool use. Here is what an error log entry looks like: Question Section Domain Skill Error Type Fix RW M1 Q14 Reading/Writing Standard English Conventions Boundaries Content gap Review independent/dependent clauses Math M2 Q18 Math Advanced Math Nonlinear functions Process error Practice graphing + algebraic check RW M2 Q22 Reading/Writing Information and Ideas Inference Wording trap Re-read exact claim before choosing Math M1 Q10 Math Algebra Systems Interface error Use Desmos intersection next time Different errors need different fixes. A content gap needs a lesson. A process error needs repeated similar problems. A wording trap needs slower reading. A pacing error needs timed rehearsal. If you do not classify mistakes, you will study the wrong things. A Reddit user who reported a 1600 on their first attempt said they took Bluebook practice tests, reviewed every missed question, figured out why they missed it, and wrote down unfamiliar vocabulary. A commenter summarized the real lesson well: the process of taking notes earned the score, not the notes themselves. Do not ask for someone else’s notes before you have made your own. The learning happens when you explain your own mistakes. How to Use Bluebook, Khan Academy, and the Question Bank Together These three official tools serve different purposes. Using them in the wrong order or without a plan is one of the most common mistakes when studying for the Digital SAT. Tool Best For Not Best For When to Use Bluebook Full-length timed tests, format familiarity, score check Teaching concepts from scratch Diagnostic, periodic retests, final rehearsal Khan Academy Learning skills, video explanations, guided practice Full-test simulation Between practice tests, after identifying weak skills Student Question Bank Targeted drills by domain, skill, difficulty Learning a concept for the first time After a diagnostic, when you know what to target The recommended workflow: Bluebook Test Preview (learn the interface) Bluebook diagnostic (find your baseline) My Practice review (identify weak domains and skills) Khan Academy lessons for weak skills Question Bank targeted drills (filtered by your weak areas) Timed mixed SAT practice sessions for pacing Bluebook retest after enough study Protect your official practice tests. If you plan to take multiple Bluebook tests over a prep period, be careful about seeing active questions in the Question Bank before you take those tests. Take at least one diagnostic before heavy Question Bank use, and use the “Exclude Active Questions” filter when it is available. Students on Reddit repeatedly warn about this overlap inflating practice scores. How to Study for Digital SAT Reading and Writing Reading and Writing has four content domains. Here is what each one covers and how to approach it, based on College Board’s domain breakdowns . Information and Ideas (about 26%) This domain tests central ideas, supporting details, evidence, inferences, and interpreting graphs or tables within passages. Study by practicing how to prove answers directly from the text. If you cannot point to specific words or data that support your choice, you are probably guessing. Craft and Structure (about 28%) This covers vocabulary in context, text structure, author purpose, and cross-text connections. For vocabulary, study context clues more than giant word lists. The test asks you to figure out meaning from the passage, not recall memorized definitions. Expression of Ideas (about 20%) This domain focuses on transitions and rhetorical synthesis. For rhetorical synthesis questions (the ones with bullet-point notes), identify the stated goal before reading the notes. The goal sentence tells you what the correct answer must accomplish. Standard English Conventions (about 26%) This is grammar: sentence boundaries, punctuation, subject-verb agreement, pronoun clarity, modifier placement, and verb tense. For grammar, learn the rules first, then drill. Random practice without understanding the underlying rule is low-value. High scorers on Reddit emphasize careful reading of prompts, last sentences, answer choices, and tiny details as the final improvement strategy. The last 20 to 40 points in Reading and Writing often come from not misreading the question, not from learning new content. How to Study for Digital SAT Math Math has four content domains, with Algebra and Advanced Math together making up about 70% of the section. Here is the breakdown from College Board’s Math alignment . Algebra (about 35%) Linear equations, linear functions, systems of linear equations, and inequalities. This is the highest-yield domain for most students below 650 in Math. Master slope-intercept form, point-slope form, and system-solving (substitution, elimination, and graphing with Desmos). Advanced Math (about 35%) Quadratics, exponentials, polynomials, nonlinear functions, equivalent expressions, and rational/radical expressions. If you are scoring above 650 and want 700+, this domain is usually where the hardest questions live. Problem-Solving and Data Analysis (about 15%) Ratios, percentages, units, probability, data interpretation, scatterplots, margins of error, and study design. These questions reward careful reading and unit tracking more than advanced math skills. Geometry and Trigonometry (about 15%) Area, volume, lines, angles, triangles, right triangles, basic trig, and circles. This domain is smaller but can be a fast point source if you know the formulas. Bluebook provides a reference sheet with common formulas. How to Use Desmos Without Overusing It Desmos is available on every Math question in Bluebook. But knowing when to use it matters more than knowing how. Problem Type Use Desmos? Why Systems of equations Yes Graph both lines and find the intersection Quadratics/functions Often Find roots, vertex, or intersections visually Tables and regression Often Desmos tables and regressions are fast Checking answer choices Yes Plug in values for quick verification Inequality regions Yes Graph and shade to confirm Simple one-step algebra Usually not Mental math or by-hand is faster Geometry/trig reasoning Usually not Conceptual setup matters more than graphing Word problems where modeling is the hard part Usually not You still need to build the equation first The practical rule: if Desmos saves time and reduces errors, use it. If it becomes a typing detour, solve by hand and use Desmos only to check. Learn Desmos during regular Math drills, not the night before the test. How Often Should You Take Practice Tests? This depends on how much time you have and where you are starting. Time Until Test Day Full-Length Test Cadence Main Focus 2 to 3 weeks 1 diagnostic + 1 final Review, top weak skills, pacing 4 to 6 weeks Every 1 to 2 weeks Skill repair + timed sections 8 to 12 weeks Every 2 to 3 weeks Foundations, drills, periodic retests Already 1450+ Fewer full tests Hard questions, careless errors, timing precision Below 1200 Fewer tests at first Content foundations and accuracy building Most students benefit from four to six full-length exams spread across their prep period. Princeton Review suggests most students take 4 to 12 weeks to prepare and should put in at least 30 minutes per day. Taking a test without reviewing it is low-value. Reviewing one test deeply is more useful than taking three tests passively. How Many Hours Should You Study for the Digital SAT? Rather than focusing only on weeks until test day, consider your total study hours. Starting Score Target Score Increase Recommended Study Hours Small (under 50 points) 20–30 hours Moderate (50–120 points) 35–60 hours Large (120–200 points) 60–100 hours Major (200+ points) 100–150+ hours Quality matters more than quantity. One focused hour reviewing mistakes is usually more valuable than several hours of passive practice. Digital SAT Study Plans by Timeline 3-Week Plan You do not have time for a complete overhaul. Focus on stabilizing your score and fixing the highest-yield gaps. Week 1: Bluebook diagnostic, full review with error log, identify top 3 weak skills Week 2: Targeted drills on those skills, Desmos practice, one timed section or full test Week 3: Final Bluebook test early in the week, error-log review, no brand-new content in the final 48 hours This mirrors the kind of realistic 3-week plan students discuss on Reddit: one Bluebook test, a missed/slow question log, targeted weak-skill work, a second Bluebook test, and last-week review. 6-Week Plan Enough time to build a weekly rhythm and see real improvement. Week 1: Diagnostic + error log Week 2: Reading/Writing weak domains + grammar foundations Week 3: Math weak domains + Desmos workflows Week 4: Practice test + deep review Week 5: Hard-question drills + pacing practice Week 6: Final practice test + test-day setup 10-Week Plan This is where genuine score growth happens, especially for students with gaps of 150+ points to close. Weeks 1 to 2: Foundations and diagnostic Weeks 3 to 6: Skill-by-skill study, one domain block at a time Weeks 7 to 9: Timed mixed sets and full-length tests every 2 to 3 weeks Weeks 10 to 12: Precision work, pacing drills, test-day rehearsal Explore more SAT prep resources for additional study materials organized by topic. Sample Weekly Digital SAT Study Schedule Day Focus Monday Reading and Writing weak skills Tuesday Algebra and Advanced Math Wednesday Student Question Bank drills Thursday Grammar review + timed Reading module Friday Desmos practice + Math review Saturday Full Bluebook practice test or timed sections Sunday Error log review and planning A balanced weekly schedule prevents burnout while keeping every tested domain fresh. Final-Week Checklist The final week before the SAT is not the time to learn new content. It is the time to consolidate what you know and eliminate logistical surprises. Review your error log, focusing on your most common mistake patterns Practice a few Desmos workflows on problem types you have struggled with Take one final timed section (or a full test) early in the week, not the night before Complete Bluebook exam setup 1 to 5 days before test day Check your device, charger, photo ID, and admission ticket If you need a loaned device, you should have requested it at least 30 days ago Sleep. Seriously. How Do You Know Your Study Plan Is Working? Don't judge progress using only total scores. Positive signs include: fewer repeated mistake types improved timing higher accuracy on weak domains reduced careless errors increased confidence using Bluebook tools Score improvements usually follow these changes rather than appearing immediately. Common Digital SAT Study Mistakes Taking practice tests too often. Tests measure progress. They do not create it. Review first, retest after targeted work. Studying “Math” or “English” too broadly. Study by domain and skill. “I need to improve Reading and Writing” is not a plan. “I need to practice Standard English Conventions, specifically boundaries” is a plan. Ignoring Bluebook tools. Mark for Review, Option Eliminator, the timer display, and Desmos are all part of the test experience. Practice with them. Spoiling official practice tests. Be careful with Question Bank active questions if you want clean Bluebook scores. Treating practice scores as guarantees. Use score trends and error patterns, not one number. Learning Desmos too late. Practice Desmos during regular Math drills throughout your prep period. No device plan. Prepare your device early. Know the 30-day borrowing rule if you need a loaned device. Not building an error log. Taking a test and moving on without reviewing it is the fastest way to waste a practice test. Classify your mistakes so you know what to fix. Best Official Digital SAT Study Resources Resource Best Use Bluebook Official practice tests Khan Academy Skill lessons Student Question Bank Targeted drills College Board Score Reports Performance analysis Desmos Calculator Math efficiency Error Log Long-term improvement Do You Need an SAT Tutor? Not necessarily. Many students reach competitive scores using official College Board resources alone. A tutor is often most useful if: your score has plateaued you struggle to identify recurring mistakes you're aiming for highly selective universities you need accountability If you're improving consistently using your error log and official resources, self-study may be enough. FAQ How long should I study for the Digital SAT? Most students should plan for 4 to 12 weeks, depending on their baseline score and target. Students with large score gaps may need several months of consistent work. Students already near their target may need only a shorter precision phase focused on pacing and hard questions. What is the best first step when studying for the Digital SAT? Download Bluebook, complete the Test Preview to learn the interface, then take one full-length practice test as a diagnostic. Everything else, your study plan, your skill priorities, your timeline, flows from the diagnostic results. Is Bluebook enough to study for the Digital SAT? No. Bluebook is best for official practice tests and format familiarity. Khan Academy notes that Bluebook is not designed to teach all tested content. Pair it with lessons, skill practice, and targeted drills from Khan Academy, the Question Bank, or another structured source. Should I use the Question Bank before taking Bluebook practice tests? Use it carefully. If you want clean practice-test scores, take at least one Bluebook diagnostic first. When using the Question Bank afterward, use filters to exclude active questions when possible so you do not accidentally see questions that appear on future practice tests. Is Desmos allowed on all Digital SAT Math questions? Yes. Bluebook provides a Desmos calculator for the entire Math section. You should learn it before test day, but remember that not every problem is faster with Desmos. Simple algebra and concept-heavy geometry are often better solved by hand. How many practice tests should I take? Enough to diagnose, practice timing, and measure progress, but not so many that you skip review. Most students use 4 to 6 over a longer prep period. Students with less time should prioritize review and targeted drills over test volume. Are Digital SAT practice scores accurate? Practice scores are useful estimates, not promises. College Board score reports include a score range that reflects natural variation. Your trend across multiple tests, your error patterns, and your timing behavior tell you more than any single number. What should I do the day before the SAT? Review your error log briefly. Check that your device is set up and charged. Pack your ID, admission ticket, and any allowed items. Do not take a full practice test late at night. Rest matters more than last-minute cramming. Studying for the Digital SAT is a system: diagnose, review, drill, retest, adjust. If building that system from scratch feels overwhelming, a structured prep platform can handle the workflow for you, combining diagnostics, personalized study paths, practice questions with explanations, full-length exams, and score analytics in one place. Start your Digital SAT prep with a diagnostic, a study plan, and practice built around how you actually learn.

title: Runway Growth Capital Appoints Michael Rovner as Co-Chief Executive Officer and Co-Chief Investment Officer
summary: MENLO PARK, Calif., August 7, 2026 – Runway Growth Capital ...
body_text: Runway Growth Capital Appoints Michael Rovner as Co-Chief Executive Officer and Co-Chief Investment Officer runwaygrowtdev 2026-08-07T12:40:43+00:00 August 7, 2026 | MENLO PARK, Calif., August 7, 2026 – Runway Growth Capital LLC (“Runway”), a leading provider of growth loans to both venture and non-venture-backed companies seeking an alternative to raising equity, today announced the appointment of Michael Rovner as Co-Chief Executive Officer and Co-Chief Investment Officer. Mr. Rovner shares both titles with founder David Spreng, and together they will guide Runway’s investment strategy and its continued expansion. Runway serves as the investment adviser to Runway Growth Finance Corp. (Nasdaq: RWAY) and to private investment funds. Mr. Rovner joins Runway from BC Partners, where he served as a Managing Director following the firm’s 2023 acquisition of Ovation Partners, the asset-backed lending and growth capital business he co-founded and led as Chief Executive Officer. His appointment adds proven leadership as Runway scales its platform and broadens the financing solutions it offers growth-stage companies, and it deepens the alignment between Runway and BC Partners Credit, which acquired the firm in January 2025. “Mike is one of the most accomplished investors in growth lending, and he shares the credit-first discipline that has defined Runway since our founding,” said David Spreng, Founder, Co-Chief Executive Officer, and Co-Chief Investment Officer of Runway Growth Capital. “He has spent three decades building and leading successful lending platforms, and he knows how to deliver creative capital solutions without compromising underwriting standards. I am confident that our partnership will make Runway an even stronger firm for our borrowers and our shareholders.” Mr. Rovner brings more than 30 years of experience spanning early and growth stage technology companies, private equity, private credit, and growth-debt lending. Before joining BC Partners, he co-founded Ovation Partners in 2012 and served as its Chief Executive Officer and head of its Investment Committee, building the firm into a provider of asset-backed lending solutions and growth capital for established companies. During that period, he also served as a board member of Vida Capital, which he co-founded in 2009 as a vertically integrated manager of insurance-related and longevity contingent assets. Earlier in his career, Mr. Rovner was a Partner and head of the financial services practice at Austin Ventures, a firm that focused on early-stage and growth equity investments in the financial services, technology, digital media, and technology-enabled services markets. He began his career in early-stage technology businesses, including Empart Technology, acquired by ARI Networks; Stanford Technology Group, acquired by Informix Software; and Mission Critical Software, which completed a NASDAQ IPO and was subsequently acquired by NetIQ Corporation. “Runway has built one of the premier platforms in growth lending, and the quality of its team and portfolio reflects the discipline David has instilled from day one,” said Mr. Rovner. “I have spent my career providing capital to growing companies, and I am honored to partner with David and the entire Runway team as we expand what this platform can do for our borrowers and investors.” About Runway Growth Capital LLC Runway Growth Capital LLC is the investment adviser to investment funds, including Runway Growth Finance Corp. (Nasdaq: RWAY), a business development company, and other private funds, which are lenders of growth capital to companies seeking an alternative to raising equity. Led by industry veteran David Spreng, these funds provide senior term loans of a target of $10 million to $150 million to fast-growing companies largely based in the United States and Canada. For more information on Runway Growth Capital LLC and its platform, please visit www.runwaygrowth.com.
