title: How Franklin Empire Stayed Independent as Rivals Consolidated
summary: Franklin Empire ranks #23 on MDM's 2026 electrical list. Here's how the fourth-generation, family-owned Montreal distributor stayed independent.
body_text: Part of Distributor Playbooks — strategy teardowns of every company on the MDM Top Distributors lists . New to the 2026 lists. Franklin Empire lands at #23 on Modern Distribution Management's 2026 Top Distributors list for electrical, one entry in a vertical MDM tracks across the biggest names in North American wholesale. What makes the Montreal company worth a closer look isn't its size relative to that list. It's that Franklin Empire is still there at all, competing as a privately held, family-run business in a Canadian electrical market that has been almost entirely swallowed by consolidators. The market it refused to sell into Canada's electrical distribution sector is roughly 98 percent consolidated , a figure that puts the country's independents in a smaller box every year. Wesco, Sonepar, and Rexel, three global platforms with European or American parent balance sheets, sit atop the market, with Guillevin close behind. Marketing groups and independents have been squeezed to roughly 16 percent share, the lowest in a decade. Against that backdrop, Franklin Empire is described in trade coverage as Canada's largest privately held independent electrical distributor, a title it has held onto while dozens of peer companies sold to national or global buyers. That is the insight worth naming plainly: Franklin Empire's competitive position is not a product line or a warehouse footprint. It is the fact that a fourth-generation family business chose to keep growing on its own balance sheet instead of taking a national's check, in a sector where almost nobody else made that choice and stuck with it. Roots in Montreal, ownership that never left the family Franklin Empire traces its history to 1942 in Montreal, and the company marked its 80th anniversary still under the ownership of the family that started it. Today the business is run by co-presidents Bernie and Clifford Backman, with Cara Backman in marketing and Les Backman in administration, a leadership bench that reads more like a family office than a distributor competing head to head with Sonepar and Wesco for the same electrical contractors and industrial accounts. That continuity shows up in staff tenure as much as ownership. Franklin Empire points to employees retiring after 50 years with the company, a retention pattern that is unusual at any scale and particularly notable in a channel where consolidation often means new ownership, new systems, and turnover every few years. The buying-group workaround Staying independent while competing against platforms with continent-wide purchasing scale requires a substitute for that scale, and Franklin Empire built one early. The company has been a founding member of AD Electrical Canada since 1993 , the buying and marketing alliance that pools volume across independent distributors, and has since added membership in AD Industrial & Safety Canada. Co-president Bernie Backman has credited that membership directly: it supplies the buying power to contend with the nationals along with networking and best-practice sharing the company would not generate alone. This is the mechanism, not just the sentiment. A buying group lets a family-owned regional player negotiate rebates and terms closer to what a Wesco or Sonepar gets from suppliers, without surrendering equity or decision rights to do it. It is the structural piece that makes the independence strategy viable rather than just admirable. Growth by bolt-on, not by greenfield blitz Where national competitors have been opening dozens of new branches a year, Franklin Empire's expansion has run through a small number of carefully chosen acquisitions of companies that share its ownership structure and culture. In 2012 it acquired Electra Supply , picking up Electra's Cambridge headquarters plus branches in London and Windsor, Ontario, and roughly 30 employees, a deal paired with an exclusive Siemens Automation and Control distribution appointment for southwestern Ontario. At the time Franklin Empire ran 20 branches across Quebec and Ontario with about 400 employees and $25 million in inventory. In February 2026 the company announced a definitive agreement to acquire O'Neil Electric Supply , a Toronto-area distributor with three branches in Woodbridge, Scarborough, and Cambridge and about 150 employees. O'Neil, founded in 1965, is itself family-run and, like Franklin Empire, a member-owner of Affiliated Distributors. Franklin Empire's own materials framed the deal around preserving O'Neil's existing teams and local expertise rather than folding the company into a centralized operating model, and around succession planning for O'Neil's ownership, the kind of continuity pitch a national roll-up rarely makes credibly. Year Milestone 1942 Franklin Empire founded in Montreal 1993 Founding member, AD Electrical Canada 2012 Acquires Electra Supply (Cambridge, London, Windsor) 2026 Acquires O'Neil Electric Supply (Woodbridge, Scarborough, Cambridge) 2026 #23, MDM Top Distributors, Electrical By 2026 the company operates 23 branches and five assembly and repair shops across Quebec and Ontario, with more than 600 employees and inventory investment exceeding $50 million. The trade-off worth naming Independence has a cost. Franklin Empire cannot fund expansion with a parent company's capital or a PE sponsor's acquisition war chest, so its growth is necessarily slower and more selective than a national's. While competitors have been opening greenfield branches at a fast clip across Canada, Franklin Empire's playbook leans on one or two acquisitions a decade, each chosen for cultural fit as much as geography. That is a real constraint on the pace of growth. It is also, on the evidence of an 84-year run under one family, the reason the company is still choosing its own path rather than executing someone else's integration plan. Franklin Empire's story is a reminder that distribution's biggest edges are rarely visible on a shelf: they live in who owns the branch network, who negotiates the buying terms, and who decides which company to buy next.

title: First United Bank & Trust President and CEO Jason Rush Named to The Daily Record’s MD500
summary: First United Bank & Trust proudly announces that President and Chief Executive Officer Jason Rush has been named to The Daily Record's MD500, a prestigious recognition honoring Maryland's most influential and accomplished leaders.
body_text: OAKLAND, Md. — First United Bank & Trust proudly announces that President and Chief Executive Officer Jason Rush has been named to The Daily Record’s MD500 , a prestigious recognition honoring Maryland’s most influential and accomplished leaders. The Maryland 500 recognizes 500 exceptional professionals across 38 diverse categories who are making a meaningful impact throughout the state. Honorees are selected for their leadership, innovation, community engagement, and contributions to Maryland’s economic vitality and quality of life. As President and CEO of First United Bank & Trust, Rush has demonstrated a steadfast commitment to serving customers, supporting local businesses, strengthening communities, and fostering a culture of excellence throughout the organization. Under his leadership, the bank has remained focused on its mission of helping individuals, families, and businesses achieve financial success while investing in the communities it serves. “The Maryland 500 represents the premier recognition platform for professional leaders who have set the foundation for Maryland’s economic success and built upon that base to chart our state’s future growth,” said Suzanne Fischer-Huettner, managing director of The Daily Record. “This is the gold standard to acknowledge the impact of innovators and icons across the Free State’s most important public and private sectors.” “This recognition reflects not just Jason’s leadership, but also the dedication of our entire First United leadership team,” said Brian Boal, Lead Director of the First United Bank & Trust Board of Directors. “Jason’s commitment to our customers, communities, employees, and shareholders continues to position First United as a trusted financial partner and community leader throughout the region.” The Maryland 500 honors leaders from a broad range of industries, including business, government, health care, education, law, nonprofits, and technology. The program celebrates individuals who are driving innovation, creating jobs, building stronger communities, and helping shape Maryland’s future. First United Corporation operates one full-service commercial bank, First United Bank & Trust. The Bank has a network of community offices in Garrett, Allegany, Washington, and Frederick counties in Maryland, as well as Mineral, Berkeley, and Monongalia counties in West Virginia. First United’s website can be located at MyBank.com. As of 6/30/2026, the corporation posted assets of $2.1 billion.

title: Symplicity vs Hiration: Which Fits Modern Career Services Better?
summary: Compare Symplicity and Hiration across career-center operations, AI philosophy, Career Compass, resume and CV support, NACE competency analysis, interview practice, student guidance, analytics, and pricing to see which platform better fits your career services goals.
body_text: For career services teams comparing Symplicity and Hiration, the decision is not simply about which platform has more features. The more useful question is what you need the platform to do exceptionally well. Symplicity is a mature career-center operating platform with particular strength in employer management, jobs, career fairs, appointments, experiential learning, outcomes, and configurable administrative processes. Hiration approaches the problem from a different direction: helping career teams scale the actual work of getting students career-ready, from resumes and NACE competencies to job-specific preparation, cover letters, LinkedIn profiles, interviews, and advisor intervention. This guide compares both platforms across the areas that matter most to career services teams, including AI, student preparation, counselor control, NACE career readiness, analytics, pricing, and operational depth. Symplicity vs Hiration at a glance Area Symplicity Hiration Stronger fit Career-center operations Deep employer CRM, jobs, fairs, appointments, recruiting workflows, experiential-learning administration and institution-level configuration Student and cohort management, assignments, resume/interview review workflows, admin controls and readiness-focused student management Symplicity for broad operations Experiential learning & outcomes Strong placement, experiential-learning and First-Destination Survey infrastructure Tracks student preparation, engagement and readiness activity, but is not positioned as institution-wide EL/FDS infrastructure Symplicity Career exploration & job search Established jobs ecosystem, skills-based recommendations and broader career-management workflows Career Compass uses student inputs, quiz responses and O*NET-backed career data to help students explore possible paths, alongside fit/gap analysis, Job Tracker and AI-supported job discovery Depends on use case; Hiration for guided career exploration Resume & CV preparation Native AI Resume Feedback is available; broader CV and JD-alignment capabilities vary by Symplicity product and CareerSet integration Resume Builder + CV Builder , institutional templates, 50+ parameter AI review, ATS checks, WHO/bullet analysis, counselor review and JD-specific resume tailoring Hiration Cover letter & LinkedIn Cover-letter and LinkedIn AI are verified through CareerSet in CareerHub, but were not publicly verified as native CSM capabilities Integrated cover-letter creation and JD tailoring plus dedicated LinkedIn profile review and optimization Hiration Interview preparation Native AI Mock Interview Feedback was added to CSM in 2026 Multiple pathways including role-, resume-, JD-, admission- and career-center-assigned interviews, Start Interview via Code, and conversational AI interviews ; also supports verbal/non-verbal analysis and AI + human review Hiration Counselor control over AI Admins can control availability of AI; deep institution-level configuration is a broader Symplicity strength Career teams can define interview expectations, evaluation methods, answer standards, attempts, leniency, cohort-specific parameters and review type, so AI evaluates students against the career center's own expectations Hiration for preparation-level control NACE career readiness NACE support was verified around First-Destination Survey standards; an equivalent resume-level competency-analysis feature was not publicly verified Dedicated analysis against all 8 NACE career-readiness competencies , showing which are demonstrated or not clearly shown and surfacing supporting evidence from the student's resume Hiration AI assistant & 24/7 student guidance Cosmo is a staff-facing CSM assistant focused on product/support questions Virtual Career Assistant provides student-facing 24/7 career guidance grounded in the institution's own resources. It can tailor guidance by cohort, surface analytics on student questions and escalate defined complex cases to counselors or campus resources Hiration Analytics, engagement & intervention Broad dashboards, reporting and outcomes infrastructure Tracks actions such as resumes created/downloaded and interviews started/completed; identifies low-scoring students or cohorts and lets admins contact those students directly from the platform Depends on use case; Hiration for readiness intervention AI philosophy AI layer has expanded rapidly since 2025, with institution controls and student opt-out; native AI now includes resume and interview feedback, skills matching and other features Built around student participation + counselor control : AI can guide rather than simply complete work, use institution-defined expectations and preserve human review where the career center wants it Hiration for counselor-controlled career-readiness AI Pricing & AI usage US pricing is quote-based; AI uses service credits, but public pricing, included credits and consumption rates were not found Supplied materials describe modular pricing based on selected products and student population, with no usage caps Hiration for pricing predictability Symplicity's established advantage is operational breadth. Its employer CRM, career fairs, appointments, experiential-learning workflows, outcomes infrastructure, reporting and extensive configuration make it a serious system of record for career services. Whereas, Hiration's product suite is centered more heavily on what students actually need to do to become career-ready, including career exploration, resume and CV creation, resume review, cover letters, interviews, student tracking, assignments and career-team workflows. What is the biggest difference between Symplicity and Hiration? The clearest distinction is that Symplicity is primarily a career-services operating system, while Hiration is built more deeply around the student preparation and career-readiness layer . Both overlap in several areas, but their product centers of gravity are different. Symplicity is particularly strong at managing: Employer contacts and relationships Job postings Career fairs Appointments Recruiting processes Experiential learning First-destination outcomes Communications Institution-specific workflows Reporting That breadth is one of its strongest advantages. Hiration concentrates much more of its product depth around questions such as: What career paths could fit this student? Which skills or experiences are missing? Is the student demonstrating NACE career-readiness competencies? Is their resume actually competitive for a particular job? What is weak about an individual bullet? Can they build a CV if a standard resume is not appropriate? Is their cover letter aligned with the role? Does their LinkedIn profile communicate the same story? Can they practice the exact type of interview they are preparing for? Can the career center define what a strong answer should look like? Can students get career guidance at 11 p.m. without relying on public ChatGPT? Which students are struggling and need advisor intervention? Those are student-readiness problems rather than employer-operations problems. That difference should drive the evaluation. How do Symplicity and Hiration approach AI differently? Both platforms now have meaningful AI capabilities. The distinction is no longer "AI versus no AI." It is what the AI is being asked to do, how deeply it sits within student preparation, and how much influence the career center retains over its behavior . Symplicity has accelerated its AI roadmap significantly since 2025. Native CSM additions include AI Resume Feedback, AI-driven skills population, skills-based job recommendations, resume/profile parsing, AI Mock Interview Feedback and Cosmo, its staff-facing assistant. Hiration's distinction is its underlying philosophy. The platform is designed around the idea that AI should work with the student and counselor rather than around them . Our product materials emphasize keeping students involved in critical thinking while allowing career teams to define the resources, expectations and parameters AI should follow. That philosophy appears directly inside the products. For example, when a resume bullet lacks context, Hiration can ask the student questions that help surface missing evidence before improving the bullet rather than simply fabricating a stronger version. For interview preparation, counselors can define the expectations against which an answer should be reviewed instead of relying exclusively on a universal AI definition of a "good interview." Hiration's interview administration also supports different evaluation approaches, attempts, reviewer models and cohort-specific expectations. The practical distinction is: Symplicity increasingly adds AI capabilities to a broad career-management system. Hiration builds the student preparation journey around counselor-controlled AI. For career teams concerned about AI replacing student thinking or creating a black-box scoring experience, that difference is substantial. Which platform provides stronger resume and CV support? Hiration goes considerably deeper into resume creation, revision and job-specific improvement, while Symplicity now offers useful native AI Resume Feedback within CSM. Symplicity's AI Resume Feedback can review areas such as formatting, structure, style and impact and provide a percentage score. The capability was introduced and expanded through its 2025 and 2026 releases. Hiration combines the feedback layer with the creation and revision process. Our resume capabilities include: Guided resume creation Customizable institutional templates AI review across 50+ parameters ATS compatibility checks Counselor review Job-description matching Missing and present skill analysis Job-specific resume versions Individual bullet analysis WHO-based bullet evaluation Contextual improvement guidance NACE career-readiness competency analysis Its WHO framework evaluates whether a bullet explains what the student did, how they did it and the outcome , rather than only checking whether the bullet sounds polished. Hiration also connects resume review directly to career readiness through its dedicated NACE Skill Analysis feature. When enabled, it evaluates a student's resume against all eight NACE career-readiness competencies: Career & Self-Development, Communication, Critical Thinking, Equity & Inclusion, Leadership, Professionalism, Teamwork and Technology. Rather than simply assigning a competency score, the system can distinguish between competencies that are demonstrated and not clearly shown , while surfacing feedback and supporting evidence from the student's own resume. That makes the feedback more useful than telling a student that they "have leadership" or "need teamwork." It helps answer a more practical question: where does the resume actually demonstrate that competency, and would an employer be able to see it? Hiration also supports a dedicated CV Builder . That matters because not every student should be forced through the same resume format. Students pursuing research, academia, graduate study, healthcare, international opportunities or other professional paths may need a CV containing areas such as publications, teaching, research, projects and academic achievements. Hiration supports both resume and CV journeys rather than treating them as interchangeable documents. For career teams, the distinction is therefore broader than which platform provides an AI resume score. Hiration brings resume creation, CV creation, document-level review, bullet-level improvement, job-specific tailoring and NACE competency evidence into the same preparation process . That gives advisors a clearer view not only of whether a student's document is polished, but whether it is actually communicating the skills and readiness the institution is trying to develop. Which platform provides stronger career exploration support? Hiration extends career readiness further upstream with Career Compass , its career exploration tool designed to help students understand which career paths may fit before they begin preparing applications. Career Compass combines student inputs and assessments with O*NET-backed career data to help students explore potential occupations in a more structured way. Students can examine career options using factors such as their interests, skills, knowledge, personality, work values and technology fit, then compare potential paths and identify gaps they may need to close. Hiration's broader career-planning capabilities also support fit-and-gap analysis across areas including domain alignment, soft skills, knowledge, technology, personality and work values, giving students a clearer view of both where they fit and where development may be needed. The larger advantage is that career exploration does not sit in isolation. Once a student has greater clarity on a direction, they can continue within Hiration to: Build or improve a resume or CV See which NACE competencies their resume demonstrates Identify skill and experience gaps Tailor their resume to a target job Create a cover letter Optimize their LinkedIn profile Discover and track relevant opportunities Practice role-, resume- or job-description-specific interviews Get additional support through the Virtual Career Assistant That makes Hiration a consolidated career-readiness platform that can support the student from initial career exploration through job preparation , rather than requiring the career center to stitch together separate tools for each stage. Symplicity also supports career exploration and has an established jobs ecosystem, including skills-based job recommendations. Its broader strength, however, remains career-management infrastructure and recruiting operations. For career centers looking specifically for a student-facing journey that begins with "What careers might fit me?" and continues through "Am I ready to compete for this opportunity?" , Hiration provides the more connected preparation experience. How do the platforms compare on cover letters and LinkedIn? Hiration provides cover-letter and LinkedIn preparation as direct parts of its student career-readiness suite. Symplicity can provide broader functionality here through its CareerSet partnership in CareerHub, but equivalent breadth was not publicly verified as one native CSM experience. Symplicity's CareerSet integration extends CareerHub with CV, job-description, cover-letter and LinkedIn capabilities. Hiration provides dedicated products for both. Our cover-letter tools support creation, job-description-based optimization and counselor review. Importantly, Hiration can also take a more directional AI approach. Instead of automatically writing the entire cover letter, the platform can give the student guidance on what needs to change so they remain responsible for developing the final content. Its LinkedIn tool reviews individual profile sections, including experience entries, rather than treating the profile only as a headline and summary exercise. For a career center trying to standardize the story a student tells across their resume, cover letter, LinkedIn profile and interview, having those preparation activities connected matters. Which platform offers stronger interview preparation? Hiration provides a much broader interview-practice environment, particularly when the career center wants to control the scenario, evaluation criteria and student assignment process. Symplicity added AI Mock Interview Feedback to CSM 9.9 in July 2026, giving students instant AI-supported review of interview responses. Hiration supports several ways to create or access interview practice: Role-based interviews Resume-based interviews Job-description-based interviews Admission interview practice Career-center-created interviews Interviews assigned to particular cohorts Interviews launched through a code Conversational AI interviews The Start Interview via Code capability is particularly useful operationally. Career teams can direct students to a specific interview using a simple code, making it useful for classes, workshops, career programs, assignments, events or targeted campaigns. Students can also continue incomplete attempts and view their progress where applicable. Hiration also supports conversational interviews rather than only static question-answer sequences. The AI can listen to the student's answer and generate contextual follow-up questions based on what was actually said, creating a more dynamic interview experience. Its interview evaluation can also analyze answer quality, speech and non-verbal factors. But the stronger institutional distinction is not the number of feedback parameters. It is who defines the standard . Career teams can configure interviews, assign them to students or cohorts, select evaluation approaches, determine attempts, combine AI and human review and define answer expectations against which the AI evaluates performance. That allows a career center to scale its own interview philosophy rather than simply adopting the vendor's. How does Hiration's Virtual Career Assistant differ from Symplicity's Cosmo? The two assistants serve fundamentally different purposes. Symplicity's Cosmo is currently positioned as a staff-facing assistant for CSM product and support questions, while Hiration's Virtual Career Assistant is designed to provide student-facing career guidance at scale . Cosmo was introduced in CSM 9.9 as a staff-facing assistant within the platform. Hiration's Virtual Career Assistant functions more like an institution-controlled career-services chatbot. Career centers can provide their own: Web resources PDFs Documents Guidance Policies Preferred resources Cohort-specific instructions The assistant can then use those materials as the basis for student guidance. It can support questions around areas such as: Career exploration Networking LinkedIn and professional branding Job-fair preparation Offer evaluation Graduate school General career planning It can also identify questions that should not be handled autonomously and route the student back toward a counselor or appropriate campus resource. Career teams can customize resources or processes for different cohorts, such as international students, veterans or particular majors. The assistant also gives administrators visibility into common student questions and emerging needs, creating another data source for deciding what workshops, resources or interventions may be needed. That means the chatbot does not simply answer questions. It extends career-center guidance beyond office hours while keeping the institution's resources and escalation rules in the loop. Hiration's supplied materials list FERPA and SOC 2 compliance and state that institutional data is not used to train external AI models. Which platform gives career teams more control? Symplicity provides deeper control over the overall operating system, while Hiration provides particularly strong control over how students prepare and how AI evaluates their work . Symplicity's configurability is a legitimate enterprise advantage. Institutions can configure fields, forms, permissions, templates, branding, workflows, modules and integrations in considerable depth. Hiration's controls are more concentrated around preparation. Career teams can: Organize students into cohorts Assign reviewers Set cohort-specific parameters Create interviews Assign interviews to specific groups Set interview expectations Determine leniency Define evaluation approaches Combine AI and manual review Manage attempts Review submissions Send engagement communications The distinction can therefore be summarized simply: Symplicity gives institutions deep control over the career-services system. Hiration gives career teams deeper control over the student preparation standard. The right choice depends on which of those is currently the problem. How do Symplicity and Hiration compare on analytics and student intervention? Symplicity provides broader enterprise reporting and outcomes infrastructure. Hiration focuses more heavily on turning preparation data into direct student intervention. Hiration can track career-readiness activities such as: Students signed up Resumes created Resumes downloaded Interviews started Interviews completed Interview reviews checked Students below defined score thresholds Cohorts requiring attention The important part is what happens after the dashboard identifies a problem. Career teams can identify students below a selected performance threshold and contact those students directly from the platform. That shortens the distance between: "We have an engagement problem." and: "Here are the students who need intervention, and here is the action we can take." This matters because career centers frequently operate with lean teams and large student populations. Hiration's account-management observations also identify limited staff capacity, fragmented tools, low post-onboarding engagement and insufficient visibility into student activity as recurring problems for career teams. Reporting is useful. Reporting connected to intervention is more useful when staff capacity is already constrained. How do Symplicity and Hiration compare on pricing? A precise US dollar comparison cannot be made from the publicly available Symplicity information, but the pricing models raise different questions for career centers. Symplicity does not publish a standard US institutional CSM price list. Public UK procurement information shows FTE-based subscriptions plus implementation and professional-services costs, but those figures should be treated as UK procurement benchmarks rather than converted into US pricing. Symplicity has also introduced service credits for AI-powered capabilities. However, that makes one procurement question particularly important: What happens to annual cost if student adoption is high? Career centers should model thousands of students using resume review and interview practice repeatedly, not simply compare base subscription quotes. Meanwhile Hiration's offers modular pricing based on the products selected and student population, with no usage caps. Based on that pricing structure, Hiration is easier to model when the objective is to encourage repeated usage rather than ration AI interactions. Which platform should your career center choose? Symplicity is likely to fit better when operational infrastructure is the central requirement. Hiration becomes the more natural choice when the team's biggest problem is delivering deeper, more consistent career preparation to more students without proportionally increasing advisor workload. Symplicity is likely the stronger fit if you primarily need: Employer CRM Recruiting administration Career fairs Experiential-learning infrastructure First-destination outcomes Institution-wide workflows Extensive enterprise configuration Hiration is likely the stronger fit if you primarily need: Career exploration before students know what path to pursue O*NET-backed career guidance Resume and CV creation Deep AI resume feedback Job-specific resume tailoring NACE competency evidence Cover-letter preparation LinkedIn optimization Repeated interview practice Institution-created interview assignments Interview access through codes Conversational AI interviews Counselor-defined AI evaluation standards A student-facing career assistant 24/7 institution-grounded career guidance Cohort-specific career support Readiness analytics Proactive student intervention For many institutions, the answer may also be both , with each system solving a different problem. What is the bottom line on Symplicity vs Hiration? Symplicity is a strong and mature career-services operating platform. Its employer CRM, recruiting infrastructure, career fairs, experiential learning, outcomes and institutional configurability are genuine strengths. But those strengths solve a different problem from the one many career teams are increasingly facing. The constraint is often no longer access to a career-management system. It is the inability to give every student enough high-quality preparation. Students need help deciding what careers fit, translating their experience into NACE-aligned evidence, creating resumes and CVs, tailoring applications, improving LinkedIn profiles, practicing interviews repeatedly and getting answers between appointments. Advisors need to maintain standards without manually handling every first pass. And career centers need to know who is progressing, who is struggling and where human attention will have the most value. That is where Hiration's model is more compelling. It combines career exploration, O*NET-backed guidance, application preparation, NACE analysis, customizable interview practice, counselor-controlled AI, a student-facing Virtual Career Assistant and readiness intervention inside one career-preparation environment. If your current platform already runs career-center operations well, you may not need another operating system. You may need a stronger career-readiness layer. title: A Change in the Prevailing Winds
summary: For several years, almost certainly dating back to the Global Financial Crisis, stock investors have benefited from a positive liquidity backdrop. Interest rates were generally low, thanks to subdued inflation, which facilitated a highly favorable supply/demand backdrop for stocks. Solid but steady economic growth amid those conditions facilitated a stable to shrinking supply of publicly traded shares, which was facilitated by buybacks and takeovers. Now, those dynamics have changed. They were a reliable tailwind for equities; now they risk becoming a headwind.

title: Average handle time: Is it costing you money?
summary: Learn how to measure average handle time and improve it with call context, smart routing, coaching, and AI tools built for service teams.
body_text: One rep is on the phone with a customer for 20 minutes. Another rep wraps a call about a similar issue in 90 seconds. But there are repeat contacts for the same issue. Your instinct tells you the same issue should take your reps roughly the same amount of time to solve, but that’s not happening. Could it be a talkative customer? Or an undertrained employee? Without a concrete number to point to, it’s hard to know where the problem is. That number is average handle time. Calculating it is the first step toward spotting patterns that quietly drain your team’s time and your customers’ patience. On its own, the number isn’t good or bad. It’s a starting point — a way to spot which reps, calls, or issue types deserve a closer look. This guide covers what average handle time means, how to calculate it, why it matters, and how to improve it. What is Average Handle Time? Average handle time, or AHT, is the average amount of time it takes your team to fully handle a customer interaction. You start tracking it from the moment the interaction starts to the moment your team finishes all the work tied to it. This includes any wrap-up after the call or conversation ends. Calculating AHT tells you how long the entire call handling process takes. Plus, it shows how efficiently your team moves through interactions. AHT also helps you determine how much of a rep’s time one interaction costs. That way, you can make better decisions about your staffing needs and budgeting. Average handle time started as a call center KPI. It was created to measure call center agent performance. But businesses can, and should, also use this metric to understand how their team is handling communication. How do you calculate average handle time? The average handle time formula is straightforward. To find out how to calculate average handle time, you need three metrics for a given period: Total talk time, or the time spent on the interaction. Total hold time, or the time the customer spent waiting or on call transfers. Total after-call work or follow-up time . ACW includes wrap-up tasks like notes, follow-up emails, or updating a ticket. Once you have those, plug the numbers into this formula: AHT = Total talk time + total hold time + after-call work time, divided by total calls handled The same logic extends to non-call channels. You divide the total time spent resolving a request by the number of interactions handled. AHT formula for texting: AHT = Total conversation time, from first message to resolution ÷ total text conversations handled AHT formula for email: AHT = Total active working time + wait time between replies ÷ total emails handled Let’s put this into practice. Average handle time calculation example Say a small team handled 200 calls last month and their time breakdown was: Total talk time: 1,200 minutes Total hold time: 200 minutes Total after-call work: 400 minutes Plug those into the formula, and the AHT is 9 minutes: (1,200 + 200 + 400) ÷ 200 = 9 minutes That number becomes the baseline they can track over time. They can compare team or individual rep performance to spot outliers. Why does average handle time matter for businesses? Here’s what calculating your AHT does for your business: Higher customer satisfaction. A high AHT can mean long waits and unresolved issues. A low one can mean customers feel rushed off the phone before their problem’s fixed. Both extremes hurt the customer experience and lead to higher customer churn. Lower operational costs and improved efficiency. A lower AHT means your existing team can handle more calls without adding headcount. This lowers your cost per interaction. More targeted coaching. A rep who’s consistently well above or below the team average is worth a closer look. It might point to a skills gap or to someone rushing calls because they’re busy with other tasks. Easier staffing and capacity planning. Knowing your AHT helps you estimate how many people you’ll‌ need to cover expected call, text, and email volume. No more following gut instincts when it comes to hiring and scheduling. 7 Ways to improve Average Handle Time Here are seven simple ways to improve the time your team spends handling communications: 1. Measure your average handle time to get your baseline Before you can bring average handle time into a healthy range, you need to know where it stands today. It’s tempting to jump straight to fixes like better scripts or more training. But without a baseline, you have no way to tell whether those changes are working. The good news is you don’t need new software to get this number. Most business phone systems already track the data you need. It’s just a matter of knowing where to look. Take Quo, for example. Inside Quo Analytics , you can view metrics like total incoming and outgoing calls and time on call. That gives you a clear, current picture of how long your team is ‌spending on each interaction. Once you’ve got the numbers pulled up in Quo Analytics, you can export them as a CSV. From there, you can calculate AHT using the formula. 💡Pro tip: Is your business on a Claude Team or Pro plan? You can connect to Claude using Quo’s Claude connector . From there, you can use Claude to help calculate average handle time at scale using natural language. Rather than exporting a CSV yourself, you can ask Claude to pull call insights and surface handle-time patterns. 2. Give reps full customer context before the call starts A large share of AHT goes toward reps re-asking questions the business already has answers to. Across hundreds of calls, that adds up to a meaningful chunk of your AHT. The fix is about technology and habit. Every time a rep learns something new about a customer or lead, they should log it in your phone system or CRM. And just as important, reps need to ‌check that information before and during the call. In Quo, there are two ways to build that context: Contact notes give reps a place to log details from conversations. It’s a freeform hub to record details like past requests and preferences. Custom properties are more structured. Set up fields for things like customer type, service history, or plan details. That way, a rep can see the essentials at a glance without digging through notes. If you use a CRM, take this a step further with CRM sync. Connecting Quo to a tool like HubSpot or Jobber auto-syncs call summaries and context between systems. This means reps aren’t stuck copying notes back and forth or switching tabs mid-call to check a customer’s history. 3. Have an internal knowledge base for reps Plenty of the inquiries reps field come from the same handful of questions. When a rep doesn’t have a quick answer on hand, the call stalls. They may even put the customer on hold to track down a teammate or dig through old emails, and that hold time gets baked straight into your AHT. Internal knowledge management takes care of this. Build out a reference document with answers to your most common questions. This could cover things like appointment rescheduling or your pricing tiers. Make it easily available so reps can answer on the spot instead of pausing the call to find out. This is especially valuable for newer team members, who won’t yet have those answers memorized and may have to lean on more experienced reps. 4. Route calls to the right person the first time Beyond wasting time, misrouted calls frustrate customers. If a call routes to someone who can’t‌ help, it might have to be transferred, which extends the call. Or the rep has to scramble to find an answer they’re not equipped to give. An unclear escalation path makes this worse, since reps may not be sure who to loop in or how. There are a few ways to fix this at the call routing level: Business-hours routing . Send calls down a different path based on whether they come in during business hours or after. This keeps a call from landing with someone who isn’t available to help. An IVR, or Interactive Voice Response , menu. This is a self-service option that lets callers route themselves to the right person or department. That cuts down on transfers before the call even reaches a rep. Ring groups. Once calls are routed, ring groups control how they’re distributed among your team. For example, you could choose to ring your senior reps first if the caller is calling with a billing issue. Or, for the fastest possible response, you can have everyone in a group ring simultaneously. On Quo, you can set this up with a drag-and-drop visual call flow builder. It’s a tool that makes it easier to map out routing, hours, and ring groups without technical support. 5. Have a call control strategy for difficult or escalated calls Staying on the phone with an upset customer because of an issue you don’t have the authority or ability to resolve just extends the call. It can also leave the customer even more frustrated than when they started. If it’s clear you’re not going to resolve the issue on the call, employ de-escalation techniques to cool things down. Then ensure you have the key details and get the caller to the right person or set up a callback . When you do hand the call off, use a warm transfer rather than a cold one. This means looping in the next person with context on who’s calling and what’s already been discussed. That way, they can hit the ground running. 💡 For more tips on handling tough conversations , check out our guide to dealing with challenging customers . 6. Use artificial intelligence to capture context and speed up callbacks When nobody’s available to pick up, what matters is capturing enough detail that the callback can resolve things quickly. A callback where the customer has to explain everything all over again increases AHT and frustrates your customer. This is where an AI voice agent like Sona comes in. Instead of the customer going to voicemail, Sona captures the message and automatically generates a call summary. When a rep needs to call the customer back, they have the context they need. For example, they’ll know what the caller wanted, their name and contact information, and any other details mentioned along the way. That allows them to get more done during the callback without starting over. 7. Train and coach reps using call recordings and transcripts Reviewing call recordings and transcripts is one of the best ways to see where calls are getting stuck. Call listening can show you why your AHT is too long or too short and whether there’s a knowledge gap, an unclear process, or a specific rep in need of coaching. To make this easier, you can ask Claude to calculate AHT per rep and flag any outliers. Here’s a prompt example you could try: “Pull my calls from [business number] from the last 30 days and calculate my average handle time. Break it down by team member and point out any outliers, meaning reps or calls that are noticeably higher or lower than the average.” If you assign some reps to more complicated calls on purpose, make sure to let Claude know. That allows you to account for unique situations rather than flagging reps unfairly. From there, use what you find to guide your coaching. Some reps might need a quick knowledge refresher, while others may require more targeted one-on-one mentoring. 💡 For more on building out a coaching approach, check out our manager’s guide to customer service coaching . Is there an industry benchmark for a good average handle time score? Some industries do publish AHT benchmarks. So it’s fair to ask whether you should aim for one of those numbers. For example, customer service contact centers usually have an average handle time of about 10 minutes . Retail companies are closer to five minutes . Business, IT, and financial services companies often take under five minutes. The trouble is, these numbers may not be a useful target for a small or growing service business. Benchmarks like these vary wildly by industry, issue complexity, and channel mix. A six-minute average for retail chatbots doesn’t reveal much about your own team’s phone consultations. Chasing a number that has nothing to do with your business can backfire. Reps start optimizing to hit the target instead of resolving the customer’s issue. Once you’ve got your own baseline, the more useful exercise is finding your outliers. Which reps or calls fall well outside your baseline in either direction and why? That’s where you’ll find the fixable problems that are relevant to your business. Track it, then fix it: Making AHT improvement stick with Quo Average handle time is a metric worth keeping an eye on. That’s why you need to run consistent call audits . Otherwise, it’s hard to know how efficiently your team is‌ serving people from day to day. But measuring it is only half the job. The other half is having the tools to do something about what you find. That’s really what a good business phone system should offer — the data to calculate your number and the tools to act once you know it. Quo does both. With Quo, you get: Analytics to establish your baseline Contact notes and custom properties so reps have context for every call A visual call flow builder to route callers to the right person the first time Call recordings and transcripts you can use to coach your team based on what’s happening on your calls Ready to see how a phone system can bring your AHT into a healthier range? Try Quo for free for seven days. FAQs What other metrics should you track to know if your AHT changes are working? AHT alone can’t tell you if a change helped. A shorter call duration could mean you’re putting speed of service over quality. That’s why you track it alongside other customer service metrics like: – First Call Resolution or First Contact Resolution. FCR measures the number of issues your reps resolved on the first call. It’s a signal of efficiency and quality service. Sometimes AHT drops and FCR drops along with it. That’s a sign the change rushed customers rather than made the process more efficient. – Customer Satisfaction Score, or CSAT. Pairing it with AHT shows whether shorter calls are also satisfying ones. – Net Promoter Score®. NPS measures how likely customers are to recommend a company to a friend or colleague on a scale of one to ten. A persistent AHT problem, whether too slow or too rushed, can eventually show up as a drop in NPS over time. How often should you review your average handle time? Match your average handle time review to seasonal shifts or new hires ramping up. You might also review the metric if you’ve implemented a new process change. What’s the difference between average handle time and average talk time? Average talk time is only one piece of AHT. It’s the time a rep spends‌ speaking with the customer. AHT is the broader metric. It comprises talk time plus hold time plus after-call work. That distinction matters because a team can have low talk time but high handle time if your average hold time or after-call work is the real bottleneck. Do you need dedicated call center software to calculate average handle time? No. A business can calculate AHT manually using free tools like Excel or Google Sheets. The tradeoff is time and effort. Someone has to pull call, text, and email durations by hand on a regular basis to keep the numbers current. A dedicated business phone system like Quo makes this much easier. Quo’s Analytics dashboard tracks average call duration automatically. It also lets you filter the results by team member, so you get the raw numbers without timing calls by hand. From there, you can export it to a CSV or connect Quo to Claude and calculate AHT at scale.

title: 9 Criteria for Sales Coaching Software in 2026
summary: Learn the 9 criteria to consider when evaluating sales coaching software in 2026, from Salesforce integration and AI to manager adoption and coaching results.
body_text: Sales coaching software has changed. It is no longer just a place for managers to take notes or review sales calls. For mid-market and enterprise revenue teams, the bigger challenge is making sure good coaching happens consistently across teams, managers, and locations. Leaders need to know whether managers are coaching, what they are coaching on, and whether those conversations are helping reps improve. That means choosing sales coaching software is about more than comparing features. You need a platform that makes coaching easier for managers and gives leaders a clear view of what is happening across the team. If you are evaluating a new platform, replacing an existing tool, or deciding whether to build your own coaching system, these nine criteria can help. What should you look for in sales coaching software? The best sales coaching software helps teams make coaching consistent, connect conversations to performance data, track whether coaching is happening, and make the process simple enough that managers and reps actually use it. For larger or distributed teams, there are nine important things to consider: Coaching session tracking Consistency across managers Salesforce and performance data integration AI-powered preparation and follow-up Support for distributed teams Manager and rep adoption Coaching effectiveness Connections to your other sales tools Whether to buy software or build your own system Here is what to look for in each area. 1. Can you track coaching sessions across your team? Start with a simple question: Can you tell who is actually being coached? For a small sales team, a leader might know this without looking at a report. At a larger company, it becomes much harder. Coaching can happen in calendar meetings, video calls, spreadsheets, documents, messaging tools, or dedicated software. Without one place to track it, leaders may struggle to answer basic questions: Which managers are holding regular 1:1s? Which reps are receiving consistent coaching? Are scheduled coaching sessions being completed? Where are reps missing coaching? What topics and skills are managers coaching most often? Look for software that gives leaders visibility into coaching session tracking without asking managers to manually report every conversation. The goal is not to track meetings for the sake of tracking them. It is to understand whether your team is getting the coaching it needs. 2. Can you create consistency without making every 1:1 the same? Consistency is one of the hardest parts of sales manager coaching . Ask ten managers to coach their reps every week, and you may get ten very different approaches. One manager reviews pipeline. Another talks through deals. Another focuses on skills. Another cancels the meeting when the week gets busy. Good sales coaching software should provide enough structure to create consistency while giving managers room to focus on what each rep needs. Look for features such as coaching templates, recurring 1:1s, structured questions, skill areas, action items, and follow-up. A good system should help your company set clear expectations for coaching without turning every conversation into a script. 3. Does it connect coaching to Salesforce and performance data? Coaching is more useful when managers can connect the conversation to what is actually happening with a rep. That makes Salesforce integration and access to performance data important when comparing sales coaching software. Managers should not have to jump between Salesforce, dashboards, spreadsheets, call recordings, and coaching notes just to prepare for a 1:1. Instead, the information they need should be part of the coaching process. Depending on the role, that might include: Pipeline created Meetings booked Opportunities created Conversion rates Revenue attainment Sales activity Individual or team goals Performance changes over time Every company measures performance differently. The important question is whether managers can easily use the data your company already cares about during coaching. Instead of asking, "How do you think things are going?" a manager can start with the data and have a more useful conversation about what is working and where a rep needs help. 4. Does AI make coaching easier for managers? AI should save managers time, not give them another tool to manage. One of the most useful ways to use AI in sales coaching is to reduce the work managers have to do before and after a 1:1. For example, AI can create a pre-read before a meeting that summarizes recent performance and highlights areas worth discussing. After the meeting, it can help capture notes, summarize the conversation, and keep track of next steps. When evaluating AI features, pay attention to what the manager actually has to do. Do they need to open another tool and ask a chatbot the right questions? Or does the software automatically bring useful information into the coaching process? Managers already have busy calendars and plenty of software to manage. AI is most valuable when it removes work rather than adding another step. 5. Can it support distributed teams? Distributed team coaching can make consistency even harder. Your sales team may work across different offices, time zones, regions, roles, and business units. The same coaching approach may not work for everyone. Your software needs to support that complexity without becoming difficult to manage. Ask whether you can: Create different coaching programs for different teams or roles Set different coaching schedules based on team needs Create shared standards across regions Give senior leaders visibility into coaching Adjust coaching as teams and reporting structures change The larger your company becomes, the more important this flexibility is. You do not need every manager to coach exactly the same way. You do need a clear standard for what good coaching looks like across the company. 6. Will managers and reps actually use it? A coaching platform cannot help your team if managers do not use it. That makes sales tool adoption one of the most important parts of the buying process. During a demo, it is easy to focus on everything a platform can do. You should spend just as much time looking at how much work those features require from managers and reps. Ask: How long does it take a manager to prepare for a 1:1? How much information has to be entered manually? Does the software automatically surface useful information? Can managers use it alongside the tools they already work in? Can reps easily find feedback and next steps? Does the software save managers time? The best software should fit naturally into a manager's workday. For larger companies, ease of use should be part of the buying decision from the beginning. It should not become a problem you try to solve after launch. 7. Can you tell whether coaching is helping? Knowing that coaching happened is useful. Knowing whether it helped is more important. Revenue leaders should be able to compare coaching activity with changes in rep performance. For example, imagine a manager spends six weeks helping a rep improve discovery skills. Can you see whether the rep's performance changes during or after that coaching? Or maybe your enablement team launches training on a new sales methodology. Can you tell whether managers are reinforcing those skills during coaching and whether performance is improving? Look for software that helps you connect: What the data shows → What the manager coaches → What happens next Not every performance change can be tied directly to a single coaching conversation. Sales performance has too many variables for that. But leaders should be able to see patterns and understand whether their coaching programs are helping reps improve. 8. Does it work with the sales tools you already have? Most enterprise sales teams already have plenty of software. You may have a CRM, conversation intelligence platform, sales engagement tool, enablement software, reporting tools, and communication platforms. Your sales coaching software should make those tools more useful, not become another place managers have to check. For example, Salesforce can show a manager what is happening with a rep's pipeline. Conversation intelligence software can show what happened on a call. Enablement software can show which training a rep completed. Coaching is where the manager can bring that information together and decide what the rep should work on next. When evaluating integrations, do not just ask whether two platforms connect. Ask a more practical question: Does this connection make coaching easier or better for the manager? That is the difference between simply sharing data and actually helping someone do their job. 9. Should you buy sales coaching software or build your own? Finally, consider the buy versus build decision. Building an internal coaching system can sound simple at first. Your company may already have Salesforce, calendar tools, call recordings, AI, spreadsheets, and internal dashboards. The challenge is keeping all of those pieces working together as your team grows. Over time, an internal system may need to handle: Manager permissions and reporting structures Recurring coaching schedules Coaching templates Session tracking Performance data AI summaries and pre-reads Next steps and follow-up Notifications Reporting Integrations Team changes Security Building your own system may make sense if your coaching needs are simple or very specific. Buying software may make more sense when you need to provide consistent coaching across a large team and building it yourself would require ongoing work from engineering, operations, or enablement. Do not compare the price of software with the initial cost of building something internally. Compare the total time, cost, and work required to maintain both options over time. Sales coaching software evaluation checklist Before choosing a platform, your team should be able to answer nine questions: Can we see whether coaching is happening consistently? Can we create coaching standards while giving managers flexibility? Can managers easily use Salesforce and performance data during coaching? Does AI reduce preparation, note-taking, and follow-up work? Can the platform support different teams, roles, and locations? Is it simple enough that managers and reps will actually use it? Can we see whether coaching is helping reps improve? Does it work well with the sales tools we already use? Is buying the software more efficient than building and maintaining it ourselves? These questions can tell you much more than a long feature comparison. Choose software that makes better coaching easier Sales coaching software should do more than give managers another place to take notes. It should make it easier for managers to understand where reps need help, have better conversations, follow up on what they discussed, and see whether performance improves. For revenue leaders, it should also answer a bigger question: Are our reps getting consistent, useful coaching across the company? As you compare sales coaching software in 2026, focus less on which platform has the longest feature list. Instead, ask: Will this make it easier for our managers to coach their people well? That is ultimately what sales coaching software should help you do. ‍

title: LegalZoom Brings Legal Services to Microsoft 365 Copilot
summary: New integration helps users access LegalZoom services and connect with attorneys without leaving Microsoft 365 Copilot MOUNTAIN VIEW, Calif. --(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 4, 2026-- LegalZoom.com, Inc. (Nasdaq: LZ), today announced it has launched an agent integrated with Microsoft 365 Copilot.
body_text: PDF Version New integration helps users access LegalZoom services and connect with attorneys without leaving Microsoft 365 Copilot MOUNTAIN VIEW, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 4, 2026-- LegalZoom.com, Inc. (Nasdaq: LZ), today announced it has launched an agent integrated with Microsoft 365 Copilot. Available through the Microsoft Marketplace, the new agent brings LegalZoom's suite of legal services — including business formation, business compliance filings, and attorney consultations — directly into the Microsoft 365 Copilot environment. The integration is designed to simplify common legal and business tasks by combining LegalZoom's deep base of legal expertise, products, and services with the productivity capabilities of Microsoft 365 Copilot. By building on Microsoft 365 Copilot LegalZoom is bringing legal support into the everyday tools used by many of the small businesses it serves. Copilot users can access legal information, review documents, explore business formation options, and connect with attorneys in the LegalZoom network without disrupting their workflow. "Small business owners shouldn't have to leave their work environment to access legal information, explore services, or connect with attorneys," said Liz Baker, Vice President Business Development, LegalZoom. "With LegalZoom inside Microsoft 365 Copilot, we are helping entrepreneurs find answers, understand their options and connect with attorney support at the exact moment they need it. This is another step toward making legal help more accessible, convenient and actionable." "Microsoft 365 Copilot is designed to help users be more productive by bringing the tools and expertise they need into their daily workflow," said Caroline Stanford, Senior Director for Microsoft 365 Suites at Microsoft. "LegalZoom's agent integration helps extend that value by giving users access to LegalZoom’s legal guidance and attorney support directly within the Microsoft 365 Copilot experience."* Guiding Entrepreneurs Through Business Formation For new entrepreneurs, LegalZoom can help them evaluate and compare different business structures, including LLCs, corporations, nonprofits and DBAs. Once a user chooses a structure, users can then seamlessly form their business and access the compliance solutions needed to help keep it in good standing, all backed by LegalZoom's 100% accuracy filing guarantee . Take a first-time founder who wants to form a business but does not know where to start. The user asks Microsoft 365 Copilot, "I want to start a business, what should I do?" The LegalZoom agent steps in and compares business structures -- sole proprietorship, LLC, corporation -- so the user can make an informed choice. Let’s say a user decides an LLC is the right fit. The agent then walks through the formation checklist covering state, business name, industry, and owners, shows LLC packages with pricing, and directs the user to LegalZoom's website to complete the purchase. When the user asks a follow-up legal question, the agent surfaces relevant LegalZoom articles. Connecting Users With Attorney Support LegalZoom also streamlines access to attorney consultations. Users can explore available attorney consultation topics, including contracts, business formation, intellectual property, employment matters and more. The agent can identify eligible attorneys within the LegalZoom attorney network that the user can choose to meet with, display available appointment times and facilitate booking consultations through either asynchronous chat or scheduled calls. The agent provides users with LegalZoom network attorney profiles, including biographies, experience and practice areas, allowing them to schedule consultations directly with the legal support they need. To help LegalZoom network attorneys prepare, LegalZoom generates an AI-powered briefing document that provides contextual information with actionable insights for attorneys on the customer before the consultation. Availability LegalZoom is available immediately through the Microsoft Marketplace for customers with a Microsoft 365 Copilot license. For more information, visit Browse Apps | Microsoft Marketplace . About LegalZoom LegalZoom is a leading online platform for legal services, transforming how individuals and small businesses navigate the legal system. By combining intuitive technology with access to experienced attorneys, whether through our vast independent attorney network or our own law firm, we offer the tools and guidance people need to confidently manage everything from business formation and compliance to intellectual property protection and ongoing business management and legal support. As AI reshapes how legal work gets done, LegalZoom is at the forefront of the human-in-the-loop approach, ensuring that the speed and efficiency of AI is always backed by the judgment and accountability of qualified professionals. With over two decades of experience and millions of customers served, LegalZoom helps individuals and small businesses navigate legal needs with confidence. For more information, please visit www.legalzoom.com . *Microsoft 365 Copilot does not provide legal advice or legal services. title: FDA Approves Tauklarify: What the New Tau PET Imaging Agent Means for Alzheimer’s Assessment

body_text: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved Tauklarify, also known as florquinitau F 18 injection or MK-6240, a new radiodiagnostic agent designed to support brain imaging in adults undergoing evaluation for Alzheimer’s disease. The approval represents another development in the growing use of advanced imaging techniques to identify biological features associated with the disease. Tauklarify is an F18-labeled tau positron emission tomography, or PET, imaging agent. It is intended to help identify tau neurofibrillary tangle pathology in the brains of adults with cognitive impairment who are being evaluated for Alzheimer’s disease. The approval was announced by Lantheus Holdings on August 14, 2026. What Is Tauklarify? Tauklarify is a radiopharmaceutical used during PET imaging of the brain. Its purpose is not to treat Alzheimer’s disease. Instead, it is a diagnostic imaging tool that can provide information about the presence of tau neurofibrillary tangle pathology. Tau is a protein associated with the development and progression of Alzheimer’s disease. Abnormal accumulation of tau can form structures known as neurofibrillary tangles. Advanced imaging technologies that can visualize disease-related proteins may give clinicians additional information when evaluating patients with cognitive impairment. According to the source material, Tauklarify is intended for adults with cognitive impairment who are being evaluated for Alzheimer’s disease. Its use is specifically focused on identifying tau neurofibrillary tangle pathology. The company has also stated that tau PET imaging can complement other diagnostic approaches, including amyloid PET and clinical evaluation. This means Tauklarify is part of a broader diagnostic process rather than a standalone replacement for other assessments. How Was the Approval Supported? The approval was supported by two blinded image interpretation studies. Together, the studies evaluated Tauklarify PET images from more than 500 participants who had taken part in three clinical trials. The participants represented a range of cognitive conditions. The clinical trial population included people with mild cognitive impairment, individuals with mild Alzheimer’s disease dementia, and cognitively unimpaired participants. Each participant received an approximate intravenous dose of 185 MBq, equivalent to 5 mCi, of Tauklarify for tau PET imaging. During the studies, independent readers who had been trained in interpreting the images reviewed the scans. The readers were blinded to clinical information and amyloid beta PET results. The scans were categorized as positive or negative for tau neurofibrillary tangle pathology and were assessed against a predetermined reference standard. In Study 1, 279 subjects were evaluated. Positive Percent Agreement among readers ranged from 80% to 88%, while Negative Percent Agreement ranged from 98% to 99%. The study also reported a high level of agreement between readers. Study 2 included 338 subjects. Positive Percent Agreement ranged from 68% to 82%, and Negative Percent Agreement ranged from 93% to 99%. Inter-reader agreement was again reported to be high. These findings provided evidence supporting the ability of trained readers to interpret Tauklarify PET images in the studied populations. Why Tau Imaging Matters in Alzheimer’s Disease Alzheimer’s disease is a progressive neurological disorder associated with declining cognitive and functional abilities. As the number of people living with the disease continues to grow, tools that can provide more information about its underlying biology are increasingly important. Tau and amyloid are two key biological features associated with Alzheimer’s disease. Imaging technologies that can identify these features may help clinicians better understand the pathology present in a patient's brain. Tau PET imaging may therefore provide information that complements clinical assessments and other biomarker-based approaches. The availability of an FDA-approved tau imaging agent could also support research into Alzheimer’s disease and the development of potential treatments. However, imaging results should be interpreted within the appropriate clinical context. A PET scan is one component of a larger evaluation, and the information it provides does not necessarily establish the complete clinical picture. Safety Information Safety was evaluated in 1,734 subjects in the Tauklarify development program. The most frequently reported adverse reactions, each occurring in at least 0.1% of participants, included headache, nausea, injection site reactions, dizziness, and abdominal discomfort. The source also identifies radiation exposure as an important consideration. Because Tauklarify is a radiopharmaceutical, administration contributes to a person's cumulative radiation exposure. The prescribing information recommends appropriate handling procedures and advises patients to hydrate before and after administration and to urinate frequently following the procedure. The source reports no contraindications for Tauklarify. There are also specific considerations involving medication use and breastfeeding. The supplied information states that CYP1A2 inducers, including tobacco smoking, should be avoided for at least seven days before Tauklarify administration. For individuals who are breastfeeding, temporary discontinuation is recommended, with pumping and discarding breast milk for a minimum of four hours after administration. Important Limitations Although Tauklarify provides another tool for Alzheimer’s evaluation, it has important limitations. The safety and effectiveness of Tauklarify have not been established for evaluating non-Alzheimer’s disease tauopathies. In addition, performance may be lower in patients who are at earlier points on the pathological spectrum. The source specifically warns that a negative Tauklarify scan does not necessarily rule out tau neurofibrillary tangle pathology. Similarly, a positive scan does not necessarily confirm the presence of the pathology. When clinical uncertainty remains, additional evaluation may be necessary. These limitations highlight why imaging findings should be considered alongside other clinical and diagnostic information rather than interpreted in isolation. What the Approval Could Mean for Alzheimer’s Care The approval of Tauklarify adds another FDA-approved option to the field of Alzheimer’s disease assessment. As researchers and clinicians continue to focus on biological markers of the disease, tau imaging may become increasingly relevant to diagnostic evaluation and research. Lantheus has indicated that it plans to continue supporting Alzheimer’s disease therapeutic programs through its Pharma Solutions business while evaluating the appropriate route toward broader commercial availability. The broader significance of the approval will depend on how Tauklarify is incorporated into clinical practice, its availability, reimbursement and coverage, competition from other imaging approaches, and how tau imaging fits into evolving Alzheimer’s treatment strategies. For patients and families, the most important point is that Tauklarify is an imaging agent, not an Alzheimer’s treatment. Its role is to provide information about tau pathology during an evaluation for the disease. Final Thoughts The FDA approval of Tauklarify marks a notable development in Alzheimer’s disease imaging. By providing a PET-based method for identifying tau neurofibrillary tangle pathology, the agent may offer clinicians additional biological information when assessing adults with cognitive impairment. At the same time, the technology has defined limitations and should not be viewed as a definitive standalone diagnostic test. Its results need to be interpreted alongside clinical findings and other relevant assessments. As Alzheimer’s research continues to evolve, tools capable of examining specific disease-related changes in the brain may contribute to a more detailed understanding of the condition and potentially support future advances in diagnosis and treatment development. Sources Lantheus Holdings, Inc., announcement regarding FDA approval of Tauklarify, August 14, 2026. Tauklarify clinical study and safety information provided in the supplied source. Tauklarify indication, limitations, warnings, and safety information. Alzheimer’s Association, 2026 Alzheimer’s Disease Facts and Figures , cited in the supplied source.
